newsitem.title: ANGOLA: UN mulls UNITA moves to avoid sanctions.
newsitem.headline: UN mulls UNITA moves to avoid sanctions.

text.p: The United Nations is deciding whether proposals by Angola's former rebel movement UNITA, accused of delaying a three-year-old peace process, are enough to avert threatened sanctions, a UN spokesman said on Thursday.

The Security Council warned it would impose sanctions from Friday unless UNITA took steps to comply with the 1994 peace accord which ended two decades of civil war against the formerly Marxist government of President Eduardo dos Santos.
UNITA responded this week.
"We have the UNITA proposals, and we are examining them," David Wimhurst, spokesman for the U.N. Observer Mission in Angola, told Reuters on Thursday.
"At this point we are finalising our position. We should be able to make our position public later today."
But an official close to Angola's peace process told Reuters he believed the UNITA olive branch would be too little for it to avoid sanctions.
"This proposal is not much better then the ones before," he said. "I can't believe the Security Council will accept these. If they can't do better then this you can expect sanctions."
Wimhurst said the U.N. decision would be announced by the Joint Commission, the body overseeing the peace process.
He would only say that the UNITA proposals addressed three key demands made by the Security Council on June 30.

The demands included handing over the vast amount of territory UNITA still controls to the government, defining the number of armed men it still controls and turning its propaganda short wave radio station, Vorgan, into a non-partisan entity.

The peace-process source said UNITA was agreeing to transform its radio station -- after a feasibility study -- but that areas UNITA was proposing to hand over were remote and surrounded by other UNITA-held territory.
The Security Council gave UNITA until August 15 to submit a plan of how to move forward on the three areas or face possible sanctions including travel and banking restrictions.
On Tuesday the Council threatened extra sanctions.
"We will consider and we will impose additional measures," said Security Council President Sir John Weston.
"Let no one say later that they were not warned. The situation is totally unacceptable."
The European Union urged UNITA on Thursday to comply.
UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, fought the government until both sides signed a peace agreement in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, in 1994.

Under the terms of the treaty the former rebels were supposed to disarm completely and hand their territory -- whose diamond mines provide the movement led by Jonas Savimbi with a hefty income -- to the government.

But UNITA still controls up to 70 percent of Angola and the government says UNITA still has 35,000 armed troops. Military analysts and diplomats in Luanda estimate UNITA troop strength at between 15,000 and 25,000.
UNITA claims to have 5,448 armed men in a new document seen by Reuters -- almost twice as many as previously admitted.
